title: How We See
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Vision is the most important of our senses, since about a quarter of the human brain is involved in processing what we see. The eye works rather like a camera: it collects light from the world, focuses it into a sharp image, and turns that image into electrical signals that the brain can read. The whole process is so fast and smooth that we are normally unaware of it, and only when something goes wrong do we notice how much we depend on it. This passage follows the path of a ray of light from an object into the brain, stage by stage.

Light first meets the cornea, the clear, curved window at the front of the eye. The cornea does most of the work of focusing, bending the light rays inwards so that they converge. It has no blood vessels, which would block the view, and it receives oxygen directly from the air and from the tears that cover its surface. It is also very sensitive to touch, which is why a speck of dust on the eye is so painful.

Behind the cornea is the pupil, the round black opening in the centre of the coloured part of the eye, which is called the iris. The iris is a ring of muscle that controls the size of the pupil. In bright light the pupil becomes small to protect the eye, and in the dark it widens to admit as much light as possible. The change takes only a fraction of a second, although it takes longer to adapt fully to darkness, which is why a cinema seems black at first.

Next the light passes through the lens, a flexible, transparent disc that adjusts the focus. When we look at a distant object, the lens becomes thin, and when we look at something close, such as a book, it becomes thick and round. This ability to change shape is called accommodation. With age the lens becomes stiffer, so that after about forty-five most people find it hard to read small print and need glasses.

The focused light then falls on the retina, a thin layer of tissue lining the back of the eye. It contains about 120 million rod cells, which respond to dim light but not to colour, and about six million cone cells, which respond to colour but need brighter light. The image on the retina is upside down, but the brain corrects this automatically. A small area called the macula contains the highest number of cone cells and gives the sharpest vision, which we use for reading.

The retina turns light into electrical signals, and these travel along the optic nerve, a bundle of about a million fibres, to the brain. At the back of the head, the visual cortex puts together the signals from both eyes to produce a single three-dimensional picture. There is a small spot where the nerve leaves the eye, which contains no sensing cells, so that everyone has a blind spot in each eye, but the brain fills in the gap so cleverly that we never notice it.

Many problems with vision can now be corrected. Glasses and contact lenses make up for a cornea or lens that is the wrong shape, and laser surgery can reshape the cornea permanently. Cataracts, in which the lens becomes cloudy, can be removed and replaced by a clear plastic lens in an operation that takes about fifteen minutes. Dr Sofia Marin, an eye surgeon, says that regular examinations are important, since some diseases, such as glaucoma, cause damage long before the patient notices any change.
